title: Causes of the First World War

match.reason: The brief combines the four long-term pressures with the assassination as the spark, but the closest bank point covers only the long-term causes and the spark card covers only the 1914 trigger, so no single point teaches the whole idea.

draft.title: Causes of the First World War
card: By 1914 four things had raised tensions in Europe: militarism, alliances, imperial rivalry and nationalism. None of them caused war alone, but together they made a major war more likely.

Militarism is building up large armies and navies, and putting military power first. Alliances are promises to support another country if it is attacked. Europe was split into two armed blocs, so a quarrel between two countries could pull in others.

Imperial rivalry was competition between powers for colonies, trade and strength overseas. Nationalism is strong pride in one's own nation, and in some cases a wish for a nation to be free of foreign rule. Both added to distrust between countries.

In June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was assassinated in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia. The alliances then drew the major powers into war within weeks.
draft.remember: Long-term tensions made war likely. The assassination in 1914 set it off.

a.q: Why did the assassination of Franz Ferdinand lead to a wide European war, not just a quarrel between two countries?
opts: Alliances drew other powers into the dispute
Every country had already planned to invade
Serbia had the largest army in Europe
Colonies had been taken from Austria-Hungary
a.why: Europe was split into armed blocs bound by promises of support, so a dispute between two countries spread to others. The assassination was the trigger, but it was the alliances that widened the conflict. Serbia did not have the largest army.
a.clue: Think about the promises of support between countries.

b.q: Germany and Britain each built more warships in the years before 1914, and each said the other was a threat. Which long-term cause does this best show?
b.why: Building up navies and putting military power first is militarism. Imperial rivalry is the tempting answer, but it is about competition for colonies and trade, not the build-up of forces. Alliances are promises of support, which this case does not describe.
b.clue: Which cause is about building up armed forces?

a.best: Alliances drew other powers into the dispute
